title: "Missing Covariate Values and Imputation"
---


```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
render_start = Sys.time()
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

Real trial data are rarely complete: a baseline lab value was never drawn, or a
questionnaire item was skipped. This article covers what EDI (Experimental Design
and Inference) does when a baseline covariate is `NA` for some subjects: it fills the
gaps (or drops the column, or stops) when it builds the model matrix. It explains why
the default imputation uses the covariates only, and why a single imputation is
enough here. It ends with what EDI does *not* handle: outcomes that are simply
missing. Censored time-to-event outcomes have their own article,
[Censored Survival Outcomes](censored-survival-outcomes.html).
It assumes you know the four steps of an EDI analysis (design, assign, record
responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html).

## The three options

Every design takes a `missingness_method` argument. It decides what happens to
covariate columns with `NA`s when the design builds the model matrix that the
inference classes use:

| `missingness_method` | What happens |
|---|---|
| `"impute"` (default) | Missing values are filled in by random-forest imputation ([missRanger](https://cran.r-project.org/package=missRanger), falling back to [missForest](https://cran.r-project.org/package=missForest)), using **only the other covariates**. |
| `"drop_column"` | Every covariate column with at least one `NA` is left out of the model. Nothing is invented. |
| `"error"` | Inference stops with an error naming the incomplete columns, so nothing is changed without your knowledge. |

A second argument, `include_is_missing_as_a_new_feature`, adds a 0/1 indicator
column for each covariate that had missing values (the default is `TRUE` for the
fixed and sequential designs). It only applies under `"impute"`.

A small data set shows all three. Forty subjects, two covariates, and `bmi` missing
for six of them:

```{r small-data}
set.seed(1)
n = 40
X = data.frame(age = round(rnorm(n, 50, 10)), bmi = round(rnorm(n, 28, 4), 1))
w = sample(rep(0:1, each = n / 2))
y = 10 + 2 * w + 0.1 * X$age + 0.5 * X$bmi + rnorm(n)
X$bmi[c(3, 8, 15, 22, 30, 37)] = NA   # BMI not recorded for six subjects

make_design = function(method) {
  des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous",
                             missingness_method = method, verbose = FALSE)
  des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
  des$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)
  des$add_all_subject_responses(y)
  des
}
```

Under the default, the model matrix holds the imputed `bmi` and the indicator
`bmi_is_missing`:

```{r impute-default}
des_imp = make_design("impute")
head(des_imp$get_X(), 4)
des_imp$get_X_imp()[c(3, 8), ]
```

With `"drop_column"`, BMI is gone; with `"error"`, constructing an inference class
stops:

```{r other-options}
colnames(make_design("drop_column")$get_X())

tryCatch(InferenceContinOLS$new(make_design("error"), verbose = FALSE),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

`"error"` is the right choice in a confirmatory analysis whose plan specifies its own
handling of missing covariates (for example, imputing them yourself before the data
reach EDI). The other two are discussed below.

## What "impute" uses, and what it does not

The imputation model sees the covariate data frame you passed to the design (plus the
missingness indicators) and nothing else. It does **not** see the outcome or the
treatment assignment. It is also seeded, by the design's `seed` if you gave one and by
a fixed seed otherwise, and it restores your random number stream afterwards. So the
same covariates always give the same imputed values, and imputing does not change any
random numbers your script draws later:

```{r imputation-seeded}
set.seed(99); u_without = runif(1)
set.seed(99)
imp_1 = make_design("impute")$get_X_imp()
u_with = runif(1)
imp_2 = make_design("impute")$get_X_imp()

identical(imp_1, imp_2)       # same covariates, same imputed values
identical(u_without, u_with)  # your RNG stream is untouched
```

(The EDI 1.0.4 release and earlier also gave the imputation model the outcome, and did
not seed it; see the section on why that biases the estimate. The change ships in the
first release after 1.0.4 and is listed under "EDI (development version)" in NEWS. A
development build installed before that release still reports version 1.0.4 but
already has the change: if `get_X_imp()` gives the same imputed values for two
different outcome vectors, your build does not use the outcome.)

## Why single imputation is enough here

The usual worry about single imputation is that it treats guessed values as if they
were observed, so the standard errors are too small; multiple imputation and Rubin's
rules exist to add the between-imputation variance back. That worry applies when the
parameter you want is defined through the variable being imputed (the coefficient on
BMI, say), or when the imputations use the outcome.

In a randomized experiment the target is the treatment effect, and the covariates are
only there to sharpen it. An imputed BMI computed from the baseline covariates alone
(the observed values, the missingness pattern and the seed) is a function of
pre-treatment data. Randomization makes it independent of the assignment, exactly
like any covariate you measured. And regression adjustment for *any* pre-treatment
covariate, even a poorly chosen or badly mismeasured one, gives a consistent estimate
of the average treatment effect with a large-sample valid (at worst conservative)
standard error [(Freedman 2008, doi:10.1016/j.aam.2006.12.003;](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aam.2006.12.003)
[Lin 2013, doi:10.1214/12-AOAS583)](https://doi.org/10.1214/12-AOAS583).
The imputed covariate is just another adjustment covariate.

A different imputation would amount to a different choice of covariate: the estimate
moves a little, but each choice's interval covers at the nominal rate. A noisy
imputation costs precision (the covariate explains less of the outcome, so the interval
is wider), not coverage. The same reasoning covers the missingness indicator, which is
also a baseline quantity. If you want an adjustment that, in large samples, is never
less precise than the unadjusted difference in means, use
[`InferenceContinLin`](../reference/InferenceContinLin.html), the
treatment-by-covariate interacted estimator of Lin (2013).

This argument needs the imputation to ignore the outcome and the assignment. The next
simulation checks it, and shows what goes wrong when the outcome is used.

## A small simulation

Each simulated trial has `n = 100` subjects and two correlated covariates; the
outcome depends on both, and the true treatment effect is 1. `x2` is missing at
random (MAR): the chance that it is missing rises with `x1`, from about 10% to about
70%, and averages about one third. Each trial is analyzed four ways with
`InferenceContinOLS`:

- `complete`: the data before any values went missing (the benchmark);
- `impute`: EDI's default;
- `drop_column`: `x2` left out;
- `impute_with_y`: `x2` imputed by missRanger with the outcome as an extra predictor,
  then handed to EDI as if complete (what the EDI 1.0.4 release and earlier did by default).

```{r sim-setup}
one_trial = function(n = 100, tau = 1) {
  x1 = rnorm(n)
  x2 = 0.6 * x1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.8)
  w  = sample(rep(0:1, n / 2))
  y  = tau * w + x1 + 2 * x2 + rnorm(n)
  X_obs = data.frame(x1 = x1, x2 = ifelse(runif(n) < plogis(-1 + 1.5 * x1), NA, x2))

  fit = function(X, method = "impute") {
    des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous",
                               missingness_method = method, verbose = FALSE)
    des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
    des$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)
    des$add_all_subject_responses(y)
    inf = InferenceContinOLS$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
    inf$num_cores = 1L
    c(inf$compute_estimate(), inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05))
  }
  X_with_y = missRanger::missRanger(data.frame(X_obs, y = y), num.trees = 100,
                                    num.threads = 1, verbose = 0)[, c("x1", "x2")]
  rbind(complete      = fit(data.frame(x1 = x1, x2 = x2)),
        impute        = fit(X_obs),
        drop_column   = fit(X_obs, "drop_column"),
        impute_with_y = fit(X_with_y))
}
```

```{r sim-run}
set.seed(20261117)
R = 200
res = replicate(R, one_trial())   # 4 analyses x (estimate, lower, upper) x R trials

est = res[, 1, ]
covered = res[, 2, ] <= 1 & res[, 3, ] >= 1
data.frame(mean_estimate = round(rowMeans(est), 3),
           mc_se         = round(apply(est, 1, sd) / sqrt(R), 3),
           coverage      = rowMeans(covered),
           mean_ci_width = round(rowMeans(res[, 3, ] - res[, 2, ]), 2))
```

```{r sim-numbers, include = FALSE}
cov_mcse = sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / R)
bias_y = mean(est["impute_with_y", ]) - 1
```

This simulation is deliberately small, `r R` trials so that the page builds in
seconds, so the coverage figures carry a Monte Carlo standard error of about
`r round(100 * cov_mcse, 1)` percentage points. Within that noise, the default
`"impute"` is unbiased and its 95% intervals cover at the nominal rate. Its intervals
are wider than with complete data: a third of the values of the strongest covariate are
guesses, and a guess explains less of the outcome than the real value. Dropping `x2`
altogether is also unbiased, but wider still. The calculation for `missingness_method`
in `?Design` repeats this with 600 trials and both linear and nonlinear outcomes.

Imputing with the outcome is the one that fails: its mean estimate is
`r round(-bias_y, 2)` too small, about `r round(-bias_y / (sd(est["impute_with_y", ]) / sqrt(R)))`
Monte Carlo standard errors, and its coverage is the lowest of the four. The bias does
not shrink as the trial grows, while the interval does, so in larger trials the
coverage falls further.

## Why imputing with the outcome biases toward zero

Treated subjects have higher outcomes. An imputation model that uses `y` to predict
the missing `x2` therefore gives treated subjects higher imputed `x2` values than
control subjects with the same observed covariates. The imputed covariate is now
correlated with treatment, which a baseline covariate in a randomized trial can never
be. The regression then attributes part of the treated arm's higher outcomes to
"higher `x2`" and takes it out of the treatment coefficient, so the estimate shrinks
toward zero. The more values are missing and the more prognostic the covariate, the
larger the bias. (Multiple imputation with the outcome *and* the assignment in the
imputation model avoids this; leaving both out, as EDI does, avoids it more simply.)

## Practical points

- Pass the covariate data frame with its `NA`s. Do not fill gaps with zeros or means
  before handing it to EDI, unless your analysis plan says to.
- Designs that use the covariates to *assign* treatment (KK matching, greedy pair
  switching, rerandomization) read the same model matrix, so the same
  `missingness_method` applies there.
- `model_formula` in an inference class chooses which (imputed) covariates enter the
  model; see [Analyzing an Experiment You Already Ran](analyzing-an-existing-experiment.html#covariates).
- The randomization test under the sharp null is valid whatever the covariates are:
  it compares a statistic across reassignments of `w`, and the imputed covariates do
  not change between reassignments.

## What EDI does not handle: missing outcomes

EDI has no method for outcomes that are simply missing: a continuous score never
measured, a binary endpoint never ascertained, a patient lost to follow-up in a
non-survival trial. Every subject needs a response, and EDI refuses to run otherwise
rather than silently dropping subjects:

```{r missing-outcome}
y_missing = y
y_missing[c(5, 12)] = NA
des_na = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = 40, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
des_na$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_na$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)
tryCatch(des_na$add_all_subject_responses(y_missing),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

(A missing `ys` is allowed only for a censored survival response, entered through
`y_Ls` and `y_Rs`.) `add_one_subject_response()` refuses `y = NA` with the same
message. If you record responses one at a time, subjects you skip simply have no
response yet, and every inference class stops with "This experiment is incomplete as
all responses aren't recorded yet."

So missing outcomes have to be dealt with before the data reach EDI, and the choice is
a scientific one, not a software default:

- **Complete-case analysis**, analyzing only the subjects with an outcome, is unbiased
  only if missingness is unrelated to the outcome within arm (missing completely at
  random, or at random given covariates you adjust for). It also changes the
  randomization: the remaining subjects are no longer a draw from the original
  design, so declare the design that matches them (for example, `DesignFixediBCRD`
  with the observed number treated) and treat randomization p-values as approximate.
- **Multiple imputation of the outcome**, with the assignment in the imputation model,
  for example with [mice](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mice), then EDI on each
  completed data set and Rubin's rules to combine. EDI does not do the combining for you.
- **Inverse-probability weighting** for dropout, or **bounds** that make no
  assumption about the missing outcomes, are not implemented in EDI.
- **Time-to-event outcomes are the exception:** a patient lost to follow-up is right
  censored at their last contact, under the noninformative-censoring assumption
  described in [Censored Survival Outcomes](censored-survival-outcomes.html).

Whatever you choose, report how many outcomes were missing in each arm and a
sensitivity analysis under a different assumption.
